svg.title: The two halves of an approval gate, its four outcomes, and the record it keeps
svg.desc: A hand-drawn anatomy of an approval gate. The first half is the policy, a function taking a tool and its arguments and returning whether approval is needed: ordinary code, so you can assert against it that this call is gated and that one is not, starting at tool granularity and moving to argument granularity for the tools where the coarse version fires on things nobody needs to see. The second half is the decider, a function taking the same call and returning a decision: a person, or something standing in for one, never directly testable, but a seam, so substituting an auto-approve or auto-deny function lets the whole flow run offline with no prompt and no human. Below, four outcomes rather than two: not gated, where the policy said no approval is needed and the call runs; approved, where a person looked and said yes, the call runs and the record says who; denied, which returns its reason as an ordinary observation and lets the run keep going; and no answer, where the request expired and the default for anything irreversible is deny. At the bottom, what the gate writes down every time: the call and its arguments, why it was gated, who decided, what they decided, and how long it sat, so the rubber-stamp rate becomes measurable rather than a suspicion. Captions record that conflating the two halves gives a gate nobody can test, then nobody trusts, then somebody disables, and that a denial which terminates the run teaches reviewers that saying no is expensive.
svg.text: What an approval gate is actually made of
Two halves that belong to different people, four outcomes rather than two, and a record of every decision.
Ordinary code, so you can assert against it: this call is gated,
that one is not. Start at tool granularity, and move to argument
granularity for the tools where the coarse version fires on things
A person, or something standing in for one, and never directly
testable. But it is a seam: substitute an auto-approve or an
auto-deny function and the whole flow runs offline, with no
prompt and no human anywhere in it.
WHAT THE GATE WRITES DOWN, EVERY TIME
so the rubber-stamp rate becomes measurable rather than a suspicion, and "who approved this?" has an answer
Conflate the two halves and you get a gate nobody can test, then a gate nobody trusts, then a gate somebody disables.
And a denial that terminates the run teaches reviewers that saying no is expensive. Make refusal cheap and it gets used honestly.
